title: One million members exposed to 'unsustainable' super funds: APRA
full_text:
The number of people exposed to unsustainable superannuation funds leapt 35 per cent last financial year as more managers in Australia's $4.5 trillion retirement savings system were deemed to be falling short of the prudential regulator's standards.
After a multi-year effort to close unsustainable super funds, the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority's latest annual report showed it failed its performance goal of reducing the number of members exposed to super funds falling short on growth, performance and efficiency standards.
Total super members exposed to questionable funds fell from 3.05 million three years ago to 763,000 in 2024-25, but shot back above 1 million in 2025-26, the annual report published last week revealed, a 35 per cent increase year-on-year.
The regulator attributed the rise to "a small number of additional funds being flagged as facing strategic challenges. APRA will continue to hold trustees to account for delivering better long-term outcomes for members," the annual report says.
APRA does not name the funds it believes are unsustainable, leaving members none the wiser about whether their fund is falling short of expectations. It does, however, publish annual benchmarks based on financial returns and fees.
In the most recent benchmarks, 11 of 141 platform trustee-directed products and one of 50 MySuper products failed. Platform trustee-directed products are ready-made options that members access through an investment platform or financial adviser. MySuper products are those assigned to an employee if they don't choose a fund when starting a job.
The industry super fund for Queensland's building, construction and civil workers, BUSSQ, was the first MySuper product to fail the performance test since it came into effect in 2023.
In a paper published in October last year, APRA outlined how it was looking at fund sustainability in an increasingly concentrated market that is making smaller funds less competitive and pushing them into a vicious cycle.
Although there has been a capital outflow from industry super funds in recent years - switching out of industry funds accelerated to a net $4.3 billion at the end of 2025, according to APRA - the largest five funds, all industry ones, hold $1.2 trillion in net assets and have a combined market share of more than 45 per cent.
In comparison, 50 per cent of funds have net assets of less than $8 billion, and collectively hold about 4 per cent of the market share.
"In general, these funds have higher member fees relative to their peers, which is likely to be impacting the competitiveness of its member offering," the paper says. "This lack of competitiveness will impact member retention and their ability to attract new members, which will lead to a slowdown in growth.
"If this trend persists, the resulting decline in membership may lead to higher fees and detrimental retirement outcomes for remaining members, as fixed fund expenses are spread over a smaller membership."
The paper concluded that these funds faced an "especially challenging outlook", and said that if the managers had no credible plan to improve the outlook for their funds, they should consider closing them.
